triples.rationale: Daniel names Joakim and Chronicles names Jehoiakim in their accounts of Nebuchadnezzar's assault upon Judah's royal house. The named ruler, Babylonian attacker and Jerusalem setting connect the narratives, while their native names and regnal dates are retained.
triples.source_text: In the third year of King Joakim of Judea, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon arrived at Jerusalem and besieged it.

target_units.text: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zechora, daughter of Nerias from Rama. He did what was evil before the Lord, according to everything his fathers had done.
In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came into the land, and he served him for three years and then revolted against him.

The Lord sent against them the Chaldeans, bands of Syrian raiders, bands of Moabite raiders, and the sons of Ammon and of Samaria. They withdrew after this event, according to the Lord’s word through His servants the prophets.
Nevertheless the Lord’s anger was against Judah, to remove him from His presence because of Manasseh’s sins in everything he had done,
and because of the innocent blood that Jehoiakim shed, filling Jerusalem with innocent blood; yet the Lord did not wish to destroy them.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him, bound him with bronze fetters, and took him away to Babylon.

triples.rationale: Both accounts describe vessels from the Lord's house being carried to Babylon and placed in the Babylonian king's temple. This identifies the sacred objects' removal, not merely a general exile theme.
triples.source_text: The Lord handed the city into his hands, together with Joakim king of Judea and a portion of the Lord’s sacred vessels. He carried them away to Babylon and deposited them in his idol-temple.

target_units.text: He carried away part of the vessels of the Lord’s house to Babylon and put them in his temple in Babylon.

triples.rationale: Isaiah warns that royal descendants will be taken into the Babylonian king's household as eunuchs; Daniel describes the selection of royal and noble Israelite youths for that court. The parallel does not establish any individual youth's descent from Hezekiah.
triples.source_text: The king told Abiesdri, his chief eunuch, to bring him some of the sons of Israel’s magnates, of the royal family and of the chosen men:

target_units.text: that they will also take some of your children whom you fathered and make them eunuchs in the house of the Babylonians’ king.”

triples.rationale: The king requires literate youths able to learn letters and the Chaldean language. The later account attributes the four youths' knowledge, understanding and literary skill to God, connecting the required abilities with their divine provision.

target_units.text: The Lord gave the young men knowledge, understanding, and practical wisdom in every literary skill; to Daniel He gave understanding in every utterance, vision, dreams, and all wisdom.

triples.rationale: The youths are to learn letters and the Chaldean language for royal service; Moses, brought up by Pharaoh's daughter, learns Egyptian wisdom. Both passages describe an Israelite figure's education within a foreign royal setting.

target_units.text: After these days the king ordered them brought in, and the chief eunuch brought them before King Nebuchadnezzar.
The king conversed with them, and among the wise no one was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. They remained beside the king.

In every matter of discourse, understanding, and education about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times wiser than the learned experts and philosophers throughout his kingdom. The king honored them, appointed them rulers, and declared them wiser than all his own men in affairs throughout his land and kingdom.

triples.rationale: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah are introduced together among the Judean youths; Daniel later returns to those same named companions to share the court's crisis.
triples.source_text: Among the lineage of Israel’s sons from Judea were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

target_units.text: Then Daniel went to his house and explained everything to his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

triples.source_text: The chief eunuch assigned them names: Daniel, Baltasar; Hananiah, Sedrach; Mishael, Misach; and Azariah, Abdenago.

triples.rationale: Daniel resolves to avoid the royal food and wine; the proposed vegetable-and-water trial and the subsequent replacement of those provisions show how that resolve is carried out.
triples.source_text: Daniel considered in his heart how he might avoid being polluted by the king’s dinner and the wine he drank, and petitioned the chief eunuch that he might not be contaminated.

target_units.text: “Test your servants for ten days, and let us be given legumes from the earth to eat, and water to drink.
If our appearance looks drawn beside the other young men eating the royal dinner, then deal with your servants however you wish.”
He dealt with them in this manner and tested them for ten days.
After ten days their appearance was good and their bodily condition better than the other young men eating the royal dinner.
Abiesdri kept removing their dinner and wine and giving them legumes in exchange.

triples.rationale: God gives Daniel favor with the eunuch in a foreign household. Joseph likewise prospers through the Lord's presence and finds favor with his Egyptian master; both accounts connect divine help with favor under foreign authority.
triples.source_text: The Lord gave Daniel honor and favor before the chief eunuch.

target_units.text: And the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his Egyptian master.
And his master knew that the Lord was with him, and that whatever he did, the Lord made it prosper in his hands.
And Joseph found grace before his master, and pleased him; and he set him over his house, and committed all that he had into Joseph’s hand.

triples.rationale: The eunuch fears that the youths will look worse than their peers and endanger him. Their healthier appearance after the trial answers that specific concern.

target_units.text: And they said to him, “We have dreamed a dream, and there is no one to interpret it.” And Joseph said to them, “Does not their explanation come through God? Tell me therefore.”

target_units.text: Then, in a vision that very night, the king’s mystery was plainly revealed to Daniel. Daniel blessed the Lord Most High,
and cried out, “The name of the great Lord will be blessed for ever, because wisdom and majesty belong to Him.
He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,
reveals deep and dark things, knows what is in darkness and what is in light, and with Him is a dwelling.
To Thee, Lord of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because Thou hast given me wisdom and prudence. Now Thou hast shown me everything I requested, to disclose these things to the king.”

triples.rationale: The presentation of the youths after the appointed days returns to the king's earlier requirement that they be educated before entering his service.

triples.rationale: Daniel's continuation until Cyrus's first year meets the same royal-year setting in which Ezra records Cyrus's proclamation concerning Jerusalem. The comparison identifies the setting without adding an unreported action by Daniel.
triples.source_text: Daniel remained until the first year of the reign of Cyrus king of the Persians.

target_units.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, so that the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians. He ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom, also in writing, saying:
“Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord, God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judea.
Who among you belongs to any of His people? His God will be with him, and he will go up to Jerusalem in Judea. Let him build the house of the God of Israel—He is the God in Jerusalem.

triples.rationale: Nebuchadnezzar's dream disturbs his sleep; Pharaoh likewise dreams and is troubled when morning comes, then seeks interpretation. Both court narratives begin with a ruler troubled by a dream.
triples.source_text: In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, the king fell into visions and dreams and was disturbed in his dream, and his sleep left him.

target_units.text: And after two full years Pharaoh dreamed a dream. He thought he was standing beside the river.
And behold, as though from the river there came up seven cows, fair in appearance and choice in flesh, and they grazed among the reeds.
And seven other cows came up after them from the river, ugly in appearance and lean in flesh, and they grazed beside the cows upon the riverbank.
And the seven cows which were ugly and lean in flesh devoured the seven cows which were fair in appearance and choice. And Pharaoh awoke.
And he dreamed a second time, and behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, choice and good.
And seven other ears sprouted after them, thin and blighted by the wind.
And the seven thin ears, blighted by the wind, swallowed the seven choice and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and it was a dream.
And morning came, and his soul was troubled; and he sent and called all the interpreters of Egypt and all its wise men. And Pharaoh told them the dream, and there was none to explain it to Pharaoh.

triples.rationale: Nebuchadnezzar summons the court's specialists over his dream, as Pharaoh summons Egypt's interpreters and wise men. Both accounts distinguish that consultation from the later divinely enabled interpretation.
triples.source_text: The king ordered the incantation-singers, magi, and sorcerers of the Chaldeans brought in to report his dreams to him. They arrived and stood beside the king.
